children: By Paul Vieira and Connor Hart
Quebecor has proposed a combination with Telus worth 31.31 billion Canadian dollars (US$21.96 billion), potentially tying up two of the biggest Canadian telecommunications companies.

The proposal represents a total consideration of about C$19.45 a share, representing a roughly 60% premium to Telus's closing share price on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Friday, according to Quebecor.

Quebecor's proposed combination would combine two complementary networks, the company said, strengthening investment capacity and competitive positioning. The tie-up would additionally create a pan-Canadian company, capitalizing on Telus's foothold in the west and Quebecor's growing presence in eastern Canada.
Under the proposal, Telus shareholders would receive C$6.35 in cash, as well as 0.17 Class B shares of Quebecor for each Telus share.
Telus on Monday confirmed its board received the unsolicited, non-binding and conditional proposal and said it has formed a special committee to review it.

"To date, this review has surfaced a number of significant risks associated with Quebecor's proposal, including the fact that more than four months after its initial proposal, Quebecor has yet to explain how what it is proposing could be approved under the current telecom regulatory framework in Canada and that a regulatory review of such a transaction would be a long and costly process for our shareholders," John Manley, chair of Telus's board of directors, said. Manley was formerly a finance and foreign minister in the Liberal government under Prime Minister Jean Chretien.

Shares of Telus are up nearly 11%, to C$13.44, in Toronto, and are on pace for the biggest one-day percentage gain in over six years, according to FactSet. Meanwhile, Quebecor's Class B, or subordinate voting, shares are down more than 12%, to C$67.32.

Quebecor is led by Chief Executive Officer Pierre-Karl Peladeau, a longtime critic of Canada's telecommunications policy and how authorities have allowed the sector to be dominated by the so-called big three of Telus, BCE and Rogers Communications. Quebecor, however, took a big step in 2024 to upend the dominance through the acquisition of Freedom Mobile, a wireless provider that Rogers had to divest as part of its takeover of Shaw Communications.

Victor Dodig stepped into Telus's top role earlier this summer, as longtime CEO Darren Entwistle retired. Former bank boss Dodig had been an independent director on the Telus board for almost four years.

Among Dodig's initial moves was to cut the company's stock dividend by more than half, with savings used to pay down debt. He has also said the company intends to focus on telecom assets and seek the sale of other noncore units, such as those in health care and agriculture. The company said the goal is to produce annual cash savings of about C$900 million starting by 2028.

Peladeau's bid for Telus is certain to pose a dilemma for federal policymakers in Ottawa, which has vowed to encourage more competition in the country's wireless sector. A government analysis this year indicated Canada among the highest prices for wireless services relative to major developed economies.

According to filings with Canada's lobbying registry, senior Quebecor representatives met last week with senior government officials--among them Michael Sabia, presently Canada's chief bureaucrat and at one time a CEO of BCE. The registry suggested the meetings focused on, among other things, policies and investments in the telecommunications and broadcasting sectors.

In its statement, Quebecor said it intends to collaborate closely with the government and regulatory authorities, "and, in this spirit, want to inform them of its approach to Telus." The company added it is prepared to make commitments to authorities regarding pricing and employment to secure approval of a potential merger with Telus.
Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joly said any transaction would face rigorous reviews from both the telecommunications and antitrust watchdogs.

Shares in the big three Canadian telecommunications providers have dropped in recent years, with Telus losing just over half its value over the last three years. In the same time period, BCE is down 45% and Rogers down 25%. In contrast, Quebecor's share price has more than doubled in the last three years.
